chapter.name: Playing with Constructions
chapter.blurb: Drawing circles, squares and rectangles with a ruler and compass; naming and rotating quadrilaterals; building rectangles from identical squares; diagonals and the angles they cut; and locating a point equidistant from two given points to build composite figures.

scope_in.item: A circle as the set of all points at a fixed distance (the radius) from a fixed point (the centre)
Drawing a circle of a given radius using a compass opened against a ruler, and why this is more reliable than a freehand curve
Corners, sides and angles of a rectangle, named using letters such as A, B, C, D, and identifying pairs of opposite sides
Rectangle properties R1 (opposite sides equal) and R2 (all angles 90 degrees); square properties S1 (all sides equal) and S2 (all angles 90 degrees)
Valid ways to name a quadrilateral by listing corners in the order met while travelling around it, in either direction
A rotated square or rectangle keeps the same side lengths and angles, so it remains a square or rectangle
Constructing a square of a given side length using perpendiculars at both ends of one side and a compass or ruler to mark the equal sides
Constructing a rectangle of two given side lengths using the same perpendicular method

Constructing a rectangle whose longer side is a whole-number multiple of the shorter side, so it divides into 2 or more identical squares, transferring the square's side length along the base with a compass

In a rectangle, the distance between a point on one side and a point on the opposite side is smallest (equal to the joining side) when the two points are equidistant from the corresponding corners, and largest (equal to a diagonal) when the points are at opposite corners
The diagonals of a rectangle join opposite corners; a diagonal splits the right angle at each of its own two end corners into two smaller angles that add to 90 degrees
Constructing a rectangle given one side and the angle-split its diagonal makes at that side (for example, splitting 90 degrees into 60 and 30 degrees)
Constructing a rectangle given one side and the length of a diagonal, using a compass-drawn arc of radius equal to the diagonal to fix the unknown corner
A diagonal splits the right angle into two EQUAL 45-degree parts only when the rectangle is a square
Finding a point that is a given fixed distance from each of two given points, by drawing arcs of that radius centred at both points and taking where the arcs cross
Using this equidistant-point method, together with earlier square/rectangle/circle constructions, to build a composite figure such as the 'House'

scope_out.item: Diameter, chord and circumference of a circle
scope_out.reason: Chapter 8 only names and uses centre and radius; it never introduces these other circle terms.

scope_out.item: A compass-only classical method for constructing a specific angle such as 60 degrees from scratch
scope_out.reason: The angle values used inside constructions (60/30, 50/40 degrees) are taken as given information, already marked in the book's own figures; the chapter never teaches how to construct a specific angle with compass alone.

scope_out.item: Rhombus, parallelogram, trapezium or general triangle constructions
scope_out.reason: This chapter builds only circles, squares and rectangles (plus one incidental triangular 'roof' inside the House figure); other named quadrilaterals are not introduced.

scope_out.item: A formal proof that the two angle-parts cut by a diagonal are related by parallel sides
scope_out.reason: The book poses this only as an 'observe, predict and discuss' exploration and never gives a proof using parallel lines and alternate angles, which is beyond the Class 6 syllabus.

scope_out.item: Perimeter and area of the constructed squares and rectangles
scope_out.reason: Those calculations belong to Chapter 6, 'Perimeter and Area'; this chapter is only about accurate construction, not measurement of area or perimeter.
Symmetry is introduced separately in Chapter 9 and is not discussed here.

scope_out.item: Placing points using coordinates or negative numbers
scope_out.reason: This chapter places every point only by distance and angle from other points; coordinates and negative numbers are introduced later, in Chapter 10.

concepts.name: Circles: centre, radius, and drawing with a compass
concepts.description: A circle as the curve formed by every point at a fixed distance (the radius) from a fixed point (the centre), and how a compass opened against a ruler is used to draw it accurately.
concepts.idea: Marking every point that is the same fixed distance from one fixed point, and joining them, traces a circle.
concepts.rule: A circle is the set of all points that are the same fixed distance, the radius, from a fixed point, the centre. To draw a circle of a given radius, a compass is opened against a ruler until the gap between its pointed tip and pencil tip equals that radius, the pointed tip is fixed at the centre, and the compass is rotated through a full turn.
concepts.example: To draw a circle of radius 4 cm with centre P, open the compass against a ruler so the gap between its two tips is exactly 4 cm, place the pointed tip at P, and rotate the pencil around P to trace the circle.

concepts.name: Properties and valid names of rectangles and squares; effect of rotation
concepts.description: The properties that define a rectangle (opposite sides equal, all angles 90 degrees) and a square (all sides equal, all angles 90 degrees), the rule for validly naming a quadrilateral by its corners, and why rotating a square or rectangle does not change whether it is one.
concepts.idea: A rectangle or square is defined by facts about its sides and angles, not by which way up it is drawn.
concepts.rule: Rectangle: R1) opposite sides are equal in length, R2) all angles are 90 degrees. Square: S1) all sides are equal in length, S2) all angles are 90 degrees. A name for a quadrilateral is valid only if its corners are listed in the order met while travelling around the shape, starting from any corner, in either direction. Rotating a shape does not change any of its side lengths or angles, so a rotated square is still a square and a rotated rectangle is still a rectangle.
concepts.example: Rectangle ABCD can also correctly be named BCDA, CDAB, DABC (going one way) or ADCB, DCBA, CBAD, BADC (going the other way), but never ABDC, because ABDC breaks the order of corners around the rectangle.

questions.a: All angles are 90 degrees, so R2 and S2 both hold. Both pairs of opposite sides are 5 cm, so opposite sides are equal (R1 holds). Since ALL four sides are 5 cm (not just each opposite pair, but all four are the same length), S1 (all sides equal) also holds. So the figure satisfies both the rectangle properties and the square properties: it is a square, and every square is also a rectangle.

questions.a: Quadrilateral 1 satisfies R1 (opposite sides equal) and R2 (all angles 90 degrees), so it is definitely a rectangle; since its two pairs of sides are different lengths, it is not a square. Quadrilateral 2 has all sides equal (S1), but without knowing the angles, S2 cannot be checked, so it cannot yet be decided whether it is a square.
s: Identifies quadrilateral 1 as a rectangle using R1 and R2

s: States disagreement with the claim

questions.a: Take a rectangle ABCD with AB = 8 cm and BC = 3 cm, and rotate it by, say, 40 degrees on the page so it looks tilted. It still has AB = CD, AD = BC (R1) and all angles 90 degrees (R2), because rotating a shape only changes its position and orientation, not its side lengths or the angles between its sides. So the tilted figure still satisfies both rectangle properties and is still a rectangle.
s: Describes a rectangle (with example side lengths) rotated to a tilted position
States that R1 and R2 still hold for the rotated figure
Explains that rotation changes only position/orientation, not lengths or angles

concepts.name: Constructing a square or rectangle of given side lengths
concepts.description: Step-by-step construction of a square of a given side length using a perpendicular and a ruler or compass, and of a rectangle of two given side lengths, using right angles at each corner.
concepts.idea: Once one side and the right angles at its ends are fixed, a compass can mark off the remaining equal sides without guessing.
concepts.rule: To construct a square of side length L: draw side PQ = L, draw a perpendicular to PQ at P, mark point S on it so PS = L (using a ruler or by opening the compass to L), draw a perpendicular to PQ at Q, and mark point R on it so QR = L; PQRS is the required square, with all four angles 90 degrees by construction and all sides equal to L. A rectangle of two given side lengths is constructed the same way, except the two perpendicular sides are marked with the two different given lengths.
concepts.example: To construct square PQRS of side 6 cm: draw PQ = 6 cm, draw perpendiculars to PQ at P and at Q, and on each perpendicular mark a point 6 cm from P and from Q respectively, using the compass opened to 6 cm; joining those two points gives the fourth side RS = 6 cm.

concepts.name: Rectangles built from identical squares; transferring a length with a compass; nearest and farthest points on opposite sides

concepts.idea: A compass can copy a length from one place to another without ever reading a ruler, and comparing equal 'how far from the corner' distances on two opposite sides reveals a pattern in the paths between them.
concepts.rule: To construct a rectangle divisible into n identical squares of side L, make one side L and the adjacent side n times L, transferring the length L along the longer side with a compass rather than re-measuring each time with a ruler. concepts.example: A rectangle that splits into 3 identical squares of side 4 cm is 4 cm by 12 cm: mark off the first square's side with the compass, then step the same compass opening along the long side two more times to mark the other two squares without a ruler.

concepts.name: Diagonals: opposite angles split by a diagonal; constructing a rectangle from a side and diagonal information
concepts.description: The diagonals of a rectangle join opposite corners; each diagonal splits the right angle at its own two end corners into two smaller angles that add to 90 degrees, with the two parts becoming equal (45 and 45 degrees) only when the rectangle is a square. Also, constructing a rectangle from one side and either an angle split at a corner, or the length of a diagonal, using a compass-drawn arc to fix an unknown point at a known distance.
concepts.idea: Once a diagonal's angle-split or its length is known, a compass turns that single piece of information into an exact point on the page.
concepts.rule: In rectangle PQRS, diagonal PR splits the right angle at P into two parts and the right angle at R into two parts, each pair summing to 90 degrees; diagonal QS does the same at Q and S. These two parts become equal, 45 and 45 degrees, exactly when the rectangle is a square. To construct a rectangle given one side and a diagonal length, draw a perpendicular to the given side at one end, then draw a circle (or arc) of radius equal to the diagonal centred at the opposite end of the given side; the point where this arc meets the perpendicular is the fourth corner.
concepts.example: To construct a rectangle with one side 5 cm and diagonal 7 cm: draw the 5 cm side DC, draw a perpendicular to DC at C, then draw an arc of radius 7 cm centred at D; the arc meets the perpendicular at the point B, giving the third corner of the rectangle.

concepts.name: Finding a point equidistant from two given points; constructing composite figures such as the 'House'

concepts.idea: Two arcs of the same radius, one from each of two fixed points, cross at the one point that is that exact distance from both.
concepts.rule: To find a point that is r cm from point B and also r cm from point C, draw an arc of radius r centred at B and another arc of radius r centred at C; the point where the two arcs cross is r cm from both B and C. Composite figures built from straight lines and circular parts can be constructed by applying this same idea and the earlier square, rectangle and circle constructions, one part at a time, in a planned order.
concepts.example: To find point A that is 5 cm from both B and C, draw an arc of radius 5 cm centred at B and an arc of radius 5 cm centred at C; A is the point where the two arcs meet.
